units.subject: Physics
units.title: Position, Distance and Displacement
objectives: Define position, distance and displacement.
Distinguish scalar distance from vector displacement and calculate net displacement.
units.body:
Position locates an object relative to a chosen origin. Distance is total path length, a scalar with magnitude only. Displacement is the change from initial to final position, a vector with magnitude and direction. Its magnitude is the straight-line separation of the endpoints and cannot exceed the distance travelled. A journey can involve a large distance but zero displacement if the object returns to its starting point. For motion in two dimensions, resolve movements into perpendicular components and find the resultant displacement.

For vector quantities, show direction and use a consistent sign convention. Diagrams should be labelled and should distinguish measured quantities, directions and reference points. units.subject: Physics
units.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities
objectives: Classify physical quantities as scalars or vectors.
Represent vectors and calculate resultants and components.
units.body:
A scalar is completely described by magnitude and unit; examples include mass, time, distance, speed, temperature and energy. A vector requires magnitude and direction; examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum. A vector is represented by a directed line segment whose length represents magnitude and arrowhead indicates direction. Add vectors by triangle or parallelogram methods. For perpendicular components, Vx = V cos(theta) and Vy = V sin(theta); add components algebraically before finding the resultant.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Equations of Linear Motion and Motion Under Gravity
objectives: Define speed, velocity and acceleration.
Apply equations of uniformly accelerated motion and interpret velocity-time graphs.
units.body:
Speed is the rate of change of distance; velocity is the rate of change of displacement; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. For constant acceleration use v = u + at; s = ut + 1/2 at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as; and s = (u+v)t/2. A velocity-time graph has gradient equal to acceleration and signed area equal to displacement. For motion in stages, calculate each interval separately. In vertical motion under gravity, use g downward and maintain a consistent sign convention.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Projectile Motion and Its Applications
objectives: Describe horizontal and vertical components of projectile motion.
Calculate time of flight, maximum height and range.
units.body:
A projectile moves under gravity after launch, neglecting air resistance. Its horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontal velocity remains constant; vertical velocity changes uniformly under gravity. For launch speed u at angle theta, ux=u cos(theta), uy=u sin(theta). For launch and landing at the same level, T=2u sin(theta)/g, H=u^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g), R=u^2 sin(2theta)/g. Maximum range on level ground occurs at 45 degrees. For a horizontal launch, initial vertical velocity is zero.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Newton's Laws of Motion, Momentum and Collision
objectives: State and apply Newton's three laws of motion.
Use impulse and conservation of linear momentum in collision problems.
units.body:
Newton's first law describes inertia; the second relates resultant force to rate of change of momentum and for constant mass gives F=ma; the third states that interacting bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other, acting on different bodies. Momentum p=mv is a vector. Impulse Ft equals change in momentum. In an isolated system total momentum remains constant. Elastic collisions conserve momentum and kinetic energy; in inelastic collisions momentum is conserved but some kinetic energy changes form. If bodies stick together, use a common final velocity.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Equilibrium of Forces, Moments, Couples and Stability
objectives: Apply translational and rotational equilibrium conditions.
Calculate moments and couples and explain centre of gravity and stability.
units.body:
A body is in equilibrium when resultant force and resultant moment are zero. For parallel forces, total upward force equals total downward force. For rotational equilibrium, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments about the same point. Moment = force x perpendicular distance, measured in N m. A couple consists of two equal, parallel and opposite forces acting along different lines; its moment is one force multiplied by perpendicular separation. Centre of gravity is the point through which resultant weight acts. Stable bodies return after a small displacement, unstable bodies move farther away, and neutral bodies remain in the new position.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Simple Harmonic Motion, Energy and Resonance
objectives: Define SHM and relate displacement, velocity, acceleration, period and frequency.
Calculate speed and acceleration in SHM and explain resonance.
units.body:
Simple harmonic motion is oscillatory motion in which acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed towards equilibrium: a=-omega^2 x. Amplitude is maximum displacement; period T is time for one oscillation; frequency f=1/T; angular frequency omega=2pi f=2pi/T. Maximum speed is omega A and maximum acceleration is omega^2 A. Kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and potential energy at the extremes. Forced vibration occurs when an external periodic force drives a system; resonance occurs when driving frequency matches the natural frequency.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Machines: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency
objectives: Define load, effort, mechanical advantage and velocity ratio.
Calculate work input/output and machine efficiency.
units.body:
A machine makes work easier by changing force magnitude or direction or the distance over which force acts. Load is the resisting force; effort is applied force. Mechanical advantage MA=load/effort. Velocity ratio VR=distance moved by effort/distance moved by load. Efficiency is useful work output divided by work input, expressed as a percentage; efficiency=(MA/VR)x100. Ideal machines have MA=VR and 100% efficiency. Real machines lose energy through friction and other effects. Work input=effort x effort distance; work output=load x load distance.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Heat Energy, Temperature, Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Capacity
objectives: Distinguish heat from temperature and define heat capacity and specific heat capacity.
Apply Q=mcDeltaT and energy conservation to heating, mixing and gravitational energy problems.
units.body:
HEAT ENERGY AND SPECIFIC HEAT CAPACITY

Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature describes the thermal state of a body. Heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder one until thermal equilibrium is approached. The source covers temperature scales, thermometers, heat capacity and specific heat capacity. Heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of a whole body by one kelvin; specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise unit mass by one kelvin.

For a body of mass m and specific heat capacity c undergoing temperature change DeltaT, Q = mcDeltaT. Use mass in kilograms, c in J kg-1 K-1 and temperature difference in kelvin or degrees Celsius. For electrical heating, energy supplied is Q = VIt or Pt, where V is voltage, I current and t time. For mixing problems, apply conservation of energy: heat lost by the hotter body equals heat gained by the colder body when losses are neglected.

The source also relates gravitational potential energy to heating when falling water loses potential energy. State the assumption of negligible heat loss and keep all quantities in consistent SI units.

practice.answer: Loss of gravitational potential energy per kilogram is gh = 10 x 630 = 6300 J/kg. Temperature rise DeltaT = gh/c = 6300/4200 = 1.5 K (or 1.5 degrees C).
practice.explanation: Equate gravitational potential energy lost per unit mass to heat gained per unit mass.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Evaporation, Boiling and Melting
objectives: Distinguish evaporation, boiling, melting, freezing and sublimation.
Explain effects of pressure and impurities on boiling and melting points.
units.body:
EVAPORATION, BOILING AND MELTING

Evaporation is the escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid and can occur at temperatures below the boiling point. Boiling occurs throughout a liquid when its saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure and bubbles form within the liquid. Evaporation causes cooling because higher-energy molecules escape from the surface. Boiling occurs at a definite temperature for a given pressure and pure substance.

Melting is the change from solid to liquid; freezing is the reverse. Sublimation is direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state. Pressure affects boiling point: reducing external pressure lowers the boiling point, while increasing pressure raises it. Impurities can alter melting and boiling points; non-volatile solutes generally raise boiling point and lower freezing point.

The source asks for experimental determination of boiling point and effects of impurities and pressure. In an experiment, heat the liquid steadily, use a suitable thermometer, record the temperature when boiling is sustained, and note the external pressure and purity of the sample.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Latent Heat of Fusion and Vaporisation
objectives: Define specific latent heat of fusion and vaporisation.
Calculate energy for temperature changes and changes of state.
units.body:
LATENT HEAT

When a substance changes state, energy may be absorbed or released without a temperature change. Specific latent heat is the energy required to change the state of unit mass of a substance at constant temperature. Specific latent heat of fusion refers to solid-liquid change; specific latent heat of vaporisation refers to liquid-gas change.

For a mass m undergoing a change of state, Q = mL, where L is the appropriate specific latent heat. If temperature also changes, combine sensible heat Q=mcDeltaT with latent heat. For ice initially below zero, first warm the ice to zero, melt it, then warm the water to the required temperature. For water below its boiling point, warm it to the boiling point before vaporising it.

Use consistent units: if mass is in grams, convert the specific latent heat units accordingly; if L is in J/kg, use mass in kg. The source includes multistage calculations and asks learners to distinguish specific heat capacity from specific latent heat.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Vapour Pressure, Humidity and Dew Point
objectives: Define saturated and unsaturated vapour pressure and relate vapour pressure to boiling.
Define humidity, relative humidity and dew point and identify measuring instruments.
units.body:
VAPOUR PRESSURE AND HUMIDITY

Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature. In a closed space, saturated vapour pressure is reached when the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation. Unsaturated vapour pressure is below the saturation value, so net evaporation can occur. A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the external atmospheric pressure.

Humidity describes the amount of water vapour in air. Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water-vapour pressure to saturated vapour pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage. A hygrometer measures humidity. Dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure and water-vapour content, for saturation to occur and dew to begin forming.

Fog and mist are suspensions of tiny water droplets near the ground; fog generally reduces visibility more strongly than mist. The source includes weather-related effects, humidity terms and a project on specific heat capacity apparatus.

practice.answer: Boiling point.
practice.explanation: Boiling occurs when saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Gas Laws and the General Gas Equation
objectives: State Boyle's law, Charles' law and the pressure law.
Apply the combined gas equation using absolute temperature.
units.body:
GAS LAWS

Gas laws describe relationships between pressure, volume and absolute temperature for a fixed mass of gas. Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume: P1V1=P2V2. Charles' law states that at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature: V1/T1=V2/T2. The pressure law states that at constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature: P1/T1=P2/T2.

Combining the laws gives P1V1/T1=P2V2/T2 for a fixed mass of gas. Temperature must be in kelvin, not degrees Celsius: T(K)=theta(degrees C)+273. The source includes trapped air columns, heated gas vessels and graph interpretation. For a changing gas state, identify which variables are constant, convert temperatures to kelvin and substitute carefully.

The ideal gas equation is PV=nRT. It relates pressure, volume, amount of gas and absolute temperature. Use consistent units for R and the other quantities.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Wave Motion and Wave Quantities
objectives: Define wave motion and distinguish mechanical from electromagnetic waves.
Calculate wavelength, frequency, period and wave speed.
units.body:
WAVE MOTION

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one point to another without net transfer of the medium. Mechanical waves require a material medium; examples include sound, water and waves on a stretched string. Electromagnetic waves do not require a material medium and can travel through a vacuum. Waves may be transverse or longitudinal depending on the direction of particle vibration relative to propagation.

The amplitude is maximum displacement from equilibrium, wavelength is the distance between successive points in phase, frequency is the number of complete cycles per second and period is the time for one cycle. Wave speed v=f lambda=lambda/T. For electromagnetic radiation in air or vacuum, use approximately 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Radio frequency is often stated in MHz; convert to hertz before calculating wavelength.

The source includes wave equations and stationary waves. Read the equation carefully to identify amplitude, wavelength, frequency, phase and propagation direction.

practice.question_locator: Second-Term Physics source, Week 8 CLASSWORK, radio-frequency wavelength calculation.
practice.question: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 21 MHz. If the speed of light in air is 3 x 10^8 m/s, calculate the wavelength.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not presented as a source-printed answer.
practice.answer: f=21 x 10^6 Hz. lambda=v/f=(3 x 10^8)/(21 x 10^6)=14.3 m approximately.
practice.explanation: Convert MHz to Hz and use v=f lambda.

practice.answer: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy without net transfer of the medium. A stationary wave is a pattern formed by superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions, producing fixed nodes and antinodes.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Properties of Waves: Reflection, Refraction, Diffraction and Interference
objectives: Describe reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference and polarisation.
Explain wave behaviour at boundaries and distinguish particle motion from energy transfer.
units.body:
PROPERTIES OF WAVES

Waves exhibit reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference. Reflection occurs when a wave meets a boundary and returns into its original medium. Refraction is a change in wave direction and speed as it enters a medium where its speed differs; frequency remains constant while wavelength changes. Diffraction is spreading around an obstacle or through an aperture and is most pronounced when the gap size is comparable to wavelength.

Interference occurs when waves superpose. Constructive interference occurs when waves meet in phase and reinforce; destructive interference occurs when they meet out of phase and reduce the resultant amplitude. Polarisation is the restriction of transverse-wave vibrations to a particular plane; it does not apply to longitudinal waves such as sound in air.

Water-wave examples show that particles oscillate about equilibrium while energy propagates. A floating cork generally moves up and down as a wave passes rather than travelling with the wave to the shore.

practice.answer: The speed decreases for the usual water-wave context described in the source; the direction may also change if incidence is oblique.
practice.explanation: Refraction involves a change in speed and, for oblique incidence, direction.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Light Waves and Plane/Curved Mirrors
objectives: Describe image formation by plane mirrors and distinguish real and virtual images.
Calculate number of images and apply the mirror formula to concave mirrors.
units.body:
LIGHT AND MIRRORS

Light is an electromagnetic wave. Reflection from a plane mirror obeys the laws of reflection: the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane, and angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. A plane mirror forms an upright, virtual image of the same size as the object, laterally inverted and apparently the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Two plane mirrors inclined at angle theta can form multiple images. For an object on the angle bisector, when 360/theta is an integer, the number of images is 360/theta - 1. Curved mirrors may be concave or convex. A concave mirror can form real or virtual images depending on object position; a convex mirror forms virtual, upright and diminished images.

For spherical mirrors, relate focal length f, object distance u and image distance v using the mirror equation 1/f=1/u+1/v under a consistent sign convention. Magnification is image height/object height and can also be related to image and object distances.

practice.question_locator: Second-Term Physics source, Week 10 ASSIGNMENT, Section A, two-plane-mirror image count.
practice.question: An object is placed between two plane mirrors inclined at 60 degrees. How many images will be seen?
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not presented as a source-printed answer.
practice.answer: Number of images = 360/60 - 1 = 5.
practice.explanation: Use the formula for two plane mirrors inclined at an angle when 360/theta is an integer.

practice.question_locator: Second-Term Physics source, Week 10 ASSIGNMENT, Section A, concave-mirror image question.
practice.question: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Describe the image formed.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not presented as a source-printed answer.
practice.answer: Using the mirror equation with a concave mirror, the image is virtual, upright and magnified. Its distance is 60 cm behind the mirror and magnification is 4.
practice.explanation: Because the object is inside the focal length, the reflected rays diverge and their backward extensions meet behind the mirror.
